newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, dollar fall; bonds up as Fed holds rates steady.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, dollar fall; bonds up as Fed holds rates steady.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks fell, while bonds rose Tuesday after the Federal Reserve surprised Wall Street by holding interest rates steady.
The dollar weakened, since higher rates would have made U.S.-based assets more attractive.
The Dow Jones industrial average fell 20.71 points to 5,874.03 just one day after closing at a record of 5.894.74.
The blue-chip index also was weighed down by a sell-off in the stock of AT&T Corp., which tumbled $5.75 to $51.50 on an earnings warning.
"We had a negative surprise from one of the bellwether stocks of all time," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,206 to 1,074 on heavy volume of 457 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

The Fed's announcement in mid-afternoon initially triggered a rally, sending the Dow up more than 30 points. A wave of selling soon followed, sending the Dow sliding more than 40 points before it reversed course yet again just moments before the close.

The Fed's decision, which had been anxiously awaited amid concern that inflation was building up, left the key federal funds rate that banks charge each other for overnight loans unchanged at 5-1/4 percent. The central bank also held the discount rate, which the Fed charges banks, at 5 percent.
Some analysts had expected the central bank to lift rates by a token one quarter percentage point, which would have been the first hike in 1-1/2 years.
Analysts said the market interpreted the Fed'sinaction as a delay of an inevitable increase after the November elections.
"Economists and traders are trying to distill all the news and ramifications of the Fed's inaction," said Eugene Peroni, chief technical analyst at Janney, Montgomery Scott.
"We had a knee-jerk rally and are consolidating to inflationary implications. It's a positive. The volatility is helping to keep excesses minimised," he said.
Analysts cited a number of reasons for the choppy finish.
"The rally in stocks and bonds pulled back partly due to the dollar," said David Shulman, chief equity strategist at Salomon Brothers, noting that the dollar fell sharply on the Fed's decision.
In the bond market, the 30-year Treasury bond rose 14/32 and its yield fell to 6.99 percent from 7.02 percent at Monday's close.
The dollar was at 1.5020 German marks in late trading, down from 1.5127 marks on Monday. The currency fell to 109.05 Japanese yen vs. 109.92 yen.
Gasoline prices ended sharply higher, giving crude oil and heating oil prices a boost, as refineries shut some gasoline producing units and bullish political news lifted the market.
Gasoline for October delivery ended 2.76 cents a gallon higher at 62.83 cents on the New York Mercantile Exchange.
October heating oil settled up 2.21 cents a gallon to 69.69 cents, while November crude oil rose 70 cents to $24.07 a barrel.

At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, October live cattle closed 1.125 cents per pound higher at 72.725 cents on tight supplies and a pickup in demand. October live hogs closed 0.05 cent per pound higher at 57.225 cents after setting a life-of-contract high at 57.450 cents earlier.
February pork belly prices also finished strong at 77.50 cents per pound, up 0.85 cent. Pork bellies are the raw material for bacon, which has seen strong demand this year.

Overseas, London's leading FTSE 100 closed 9.2 points lower at 3,910.5, as decliners outnumbered advancers by a margin of about five to four. In Tokyo, the key Nikkei 225 average closed up 59.75 points at 21,171.99.
